title: Advent Ledger
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
subtopic: Fifth Amendment act-of-production privilege and immunity
stem:
After a fatal hit-and-run outside a winter pageant rehearsal, a state grand jury learned that Stephen, the key suspect, might have kept a hand-lettered Advent gratitude ledger describing his late-night errands. Instead of asking Stephen questions, the grand jury served him with a subpoena duces tecum requiring him to produce any such ledger. The subpoena stated that the grand jury sought only the ledger itself. Stephen refused, invoking his Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.

Under what circumstances, if any, may the grand jury compel Stephen to produce the ledger over that assertion?
call: Under what circumstances, if any, may the grand jury compel Stephen to produce the ledger over that assertion?

choices.A: It may not compel production of a personal devotional ledger under any circumstances.
choices.B: It may compel production without granting immunity, because Stephen was not compelled to create the ledger.
choices.C: It may compel production only if Stephen is granted use and derivative use immunity from the act of production.
choices.D: It may compel production only if Stephen is granted transactional immunity.

rightExplanation:
C is correct. The call asks how the grand jury may compel production over a Fifth Amendment assertion. The answer is not “never,” and it is not “only with total immunity from prosecution.” The needed protection is use and derivative use immunity for the act of production.

Gold Key: A subpoena for a preexisting private writing does not compel the writing’s contents, but producing it can be testimonial when production admits existence, possession, or authenticity. Use and derivative use immunity is enough to compel that act; transactional immunity is not required.

Silver Key: Read the choices as an immunity ladder: no immunity, use-and-derivative immunity, transactional immunity, or no compulsion ever. The middle protection is the exam answer when the privilege is real but can be displaced.

c3.label: CUT phase
c3.text: No choice is student-accessibly false from grammar alone. The item is anchor-dependent. The student should not fake structure.

c3.label: Choice A
c3.text: Cut after the Gold Key. The phrase “under any circumstances” is an absolute endpoint. The Gold Key supplies the exception: use and derivative use immunity can compel production.

c3.label: Choice B
c3.text: Cut after the Gold Key. The choice focuses on the content-creation frame. The call asks about compelled production. That is a wrong-frame half-truth.

c3.label: Choice D
c3.text: Cut after the Gold Key. “Only transactional immunity” demands more protection than the privilege requires.

c3.label: CLASH phase
c3.text: The apparent clash is an immunity ladder: no immunity, use-and-derivative immunity, transactional immunity, never compel.

c3.label: CALL phase
c3.text: Apply the Gold Key. The protection must match the Fifth Amendment privilege. That points to C.

studentScript: This is an anchor ladder. The subpoena asks for production, not authorship. Production can testify, but use and derivative use immunity is enough. Pick C.

A.signal: The phrase 'under any circumstances' is an endpoint in an immunity ladder.
A.lawyer: The privilege may be displaced by use and derivative use immunity for compelled testimonial production.

B.signal: The choice answers whether Stephen was compelled to create the ledger, not whether producing it is testimonial.
B.lawyer: The act of production can itself communicate existence, possession, or authenticity.

C.signal: The middle immunity level matches the privilege once the Gold Key is supplied.
C.lawyer: Use and derivative use immunity is constitutionally sufficient; transactional immunity is not required.

D.signal: The word 'only' demands broader protection than the privilege requires.
D.lawyer: Transactional immunity is broader than use and derivative use immunity and is not constitutionally required.

goldKeys.statement: A subpoena for a preexisting private writing does not compel the writing’s contents, but producing it can be testimonial when production admits existence, possession, or authenticity. Use and derivative use immunity is enough to compel that act; transactional immunity is not required.
goldKeys.trigger: a grand jury asks a suspect to produce a possibly existing personal writing rather than answer questions
goldKeys.unlocks: the content-versus-production trap and the use-and-derivative-use versus transactional-immunity ladder
goldKeys.authority: Fisher v. United States; United States v. Doe; Kastigar v. United States; Murphy v. Waterfront Commission

silverKeys.statement: Read the choices as an immunity ladder: none, use-and-derivative, transactional, or never. The middle protection usually wins when the call asks how compulsion can happen, not whether the suspect wrote the item voluntarily.
silverKeys.trigger: answer choices escalate from no immunity to use-and-derivative immunity to transactional immunity to no compulsion ever
silverKeys.unlocks: the four-choice ladder that tempts students to pick either no protection or total protection

remediation.title: Act of production is the testimony
remediation.signal: A subpoena asks a suspect for a document the government only thinks may exist.
remediation.studentMove: Separate the document’s preexisting contents from the act of producing it.
remediation.tinyRule: Use and derivative use immunity is enough to compel a testimonial act of production.
remediation.trap: No-immunity and transactional-immunity endpoints both overshoot the privilege.
